stimulus.text: Martin Waldseemuller's world map, published in 1507, was the first map to use the name America for the lands across the Atlantic Ocean. It shows the western lands as a separate landmass. The portrait of Amerigo Vespucci stands beside one globe at the top of the map, and the portrait of the ancient geographer Ptolemy stands beside the other globe.
stimulus.source_note: Waldseemuller map, 1507, public domain; Library of Congress.

books.section: Portugal and Spain Lead the Way

stem: Why did Waldseemuller name the western lands America, after Amerigo Vespucci?

options.text: Vespucci paid for the printing of the map in Saint-Die.
options.misconception: Assumes Vespucci funded the map, but no evidence ties him to its printing.

options.text: The Spanish crown ordered the name to honor a royal favorite.
options.misconception: Credits a royal order that never existed; the name came from mapmakers, not the crown.

options.text: Columbus asked that the lands be named for Vespucci.
options.misconception: Puts words in the mouth of Columbus, who believed he had reached Asia.

options.text: Vespucci argued the lands were a new world, and mapmakers agreed.

rationales.general:
1. Look at the map. Vespucci stands beside the globe at the top, honored as a source.
2. Ask what Vespucci claimed. His letters argued that the lands across the Atlantic were a new world, not Asia.
3. Ask what mapmakers did with that claim. Waldseemuller accepted it and gave the lands a new name from Vespucci, a thank-you written on the map itself.
4. Conclude. The name records whose idea the mapmakers trusted.
Remember: when a map honors a person, ask what idea that person supplied.
rationales.A: Vespucci did not pay for the map; Waldseemuller and his partners printed it in Saint-Die, and the name came from Vespucci's writings.
rationales.B: The Spanish crown did not order the name, and the map was printed in the Duchy of Lorraine, outside Spanish control.
rationales.C: Columbus believed until his death that he had reached Asia, so he would not have asked for a name that marked a new continent.
rationales.D: Vespucci's letters argued the lands were a new world, and Waldseemuller followed that claim by naming them America.

figures.caption: Martin Waldseemuller's world map of 1507, the first map to name the western lands America
figures.alt: A 1507 world map in twelve sheets showing Europe, Africa, Asia, and a long western landmass labeled America on the left side
